because empires are loud — they build walls and stamp seals and rename things in languages that coat their tongues with the taste of authority. And when they fall, the silence they leave behind is so deafening that your ears believe that the sound is of a world that has ended.

Tarim Shaiel is a realm of deep myth. The legends, the old gods, the tyrants, none of it halts the life-blood that is trade roads. Only the end of everything could stem that tide. But the end may be coming
What do you do when the world is very certain who you are — and you're not?
Read this to your players when pitching the campaign.

Tarim Shaiel is a dark fantasy campaign set in a world that carries the weight of its past like a wound that never quite closed. It is a world with opinions: about consequence, about history, about the people who shaped it and the debts that haven't been settled. Your characters are people that world has decided something about. Whether those decisions are right, whether they fit, and what you choose to become in their shadow: that is the campaign. Expect doubt. Expect hard choices with no clean answers. Expect consequences that persist, people who have every right to be complicated about you, and moments of recognition that land harder than any fight. This is not a campaign about heroism. It is a campaign about what heroism actually costs. And who pays.
Fantasy · Character Choices · Weighty · Intimate · Consequential
Your characters carry significance they didn't choose and can't fully account for. The name means something to the world. Whether it means the same thing to you is the question.
This is not a campaign about certainty. It is a campaign about making choices anyway: under pressure, with incomplete information, knowing the cost may not be clear until later.
Every action here casts a shadow. The campaign asks players to sit with outcomes, to let them mean something rather than immediately move past them.

Liberation is not the same as peace, and peace is not the same as justice. The world the characters move through is still working that out. Some of it is raw. Some of it has calcified into myth. None of it is finished.
The characters are significant. That significance was not free. Someone paid. Some of them are still paying. The campaign, over time, asks its characters to look at that directly.
[GM: Confirm and add to this list. Suggestions below — use what fits your table's frame of reference.]
[Add 2–3 more — fiction, film, or other RPGs that set the right tonal expectation for your table]

The throughlines to look for: moral complexity without nihilism, consequence that compounds, characters who are genuinely changed by what they do, worlds with a deep and lived-in history that wasn't built for the protagonists.
Player-facing. One page. Sets the world without revealing the premise.

The world is old and complicated in the way that only centuries of unresolved consequence can make a place. What was once an empire is now history, fallen not cleanly, but in pieces, leaving fractures that became regions, became cultures, became arguments that haven't been settled in a very long time.

The world players enter is rich with those arguments. Eight distinct regions, each shaped by its own reckoning with the past. The peoples here are not waiting for anything. They have been building, trading, recovering, and arguing on their own terms, in their own time, with their own sense of who owes what to whom. They have long memories, and they hold them differently: some calcified into grievance, some softened into myth, some interrogated rigorously and still unresolved.

Magic moves through the world along channels most people don't have names for. What they have instead are habits: roads avoided at certain hours, markets where certain goods carry a weight the merchants don't discuss, places that feel wrong in ways that resist explanation. Something has been quietly unreliable for long enough that most people have learned to rationalize it. A few haven't. Some of them are watching.

The characters move through this world carrying a weight: of being significant to people they've never met, of factions with agendas, of histories that name them without asking. The world has already decided something about who they are. Some of those decisions are flattering. Some condemn. Some are simply wrong in ways that matter. None of them asked first.

Tarim Shaiel is about what the characters do inside that pressure. About the doubt, the gap between what the world says and what the characters can actually verify about themselves. About hard choices made without the certainty that would make them easier. About whether it is possible to choose who you are when something larger has already tried to do it for you.
The campaign is long. The world is alive and opinionated. The best moments will not be victories. They will be recognitions.
All ancestries and classes from the Daggerheart Core Rulebook are available in Tarim Shaiel. The world is populated and diverse; no door is closed on the basis of what your character is.
What matters more than ancestry or class is
The characters of Tarim Shaiel are defined less by what they can do and more by
they meet the world. When building your character, sit with this question before you touch a character sheet:
What is your character's essential method: the way they change things, the thing that makes them distinctly themselves?

Are they someone who meets obstacles with force and decisive action? Who uncovers truths others wouldn't look for? Who breaks structures rather than reforming them, or mediates where others refuse to, or gives of themselves without reservation? Are they a careful observer, or a keeper of what others would destroy, or someone who operates through misdirection and patience?
That method is your character's spine. In this campaign, it is also their defining doubt. The question they will not be able to stop turning over. Come to Session Zero with a sense of it.
A character creation guide with expanded guidance on approaches will be provided at Session Zero.
Follow these principles to stay in the right relationship with the campaign's themes. They are not rules. They are the mindset that makes the campaign work.

Your character's uncertainty is not a problem to solve in session one. It is the experience. Let it stay unresolved for as long as it needs to. Reaching for certainty too early forecloses the campaign's best questions.
The world's verdict is not the last word.

What factions, strangers, and histories say about your character is information: sometimes useful, sometimes wrong, sometimes both at once. You don't have to accept it. You don't have to reject it either. What you do with it is character.
Whatever your character carries, whatever weight attaches to their name, their decisions
belong to them. The past is context. The present is character. Play from there.

This campaign rewards players who let outcomes mean something, who don't immediately move to fix or escape what happened, but instead live in what it costs. The sessions here are built around that space. Use it.
Look directly at the hard things.

When a scene makes you want to look away from something your character did, or enabled, or benefited from: look at it instead. That discomfort is the campaign working as intended. The best moments in Tarim Shaiel come from characters who don't flinch.
Use these principles to run a campaign that earns its themes.

Every faction, every NPC, every community has already formed a view of the characters before they arrive. Some of those views contradict each other. Let that conflict be present and unresolved. The world is not neutral about these people.

No single source has the complete picture. Spread fragments across the world: in records, in oral traditions, in reactions, in things that haven't been said yet. Let the characters piece it together slowly. The full picture, when it forms, should feel

Answers will come. Pace them so they land. What a character discovers through action and consequence will mean more than what they're told. Give the doubt enough time to do its work, and the clarity, when it arrives, will feel like it belongs.

The campaign's best moments are not always battles. They are often recognitions: when a character understands what their methods actually cost, when they meet someone who inherited that cost, when something they did in a previous session arrives changed. Build toward these with patience. Let them land without commentary.

What the characters are, what they do, and what that means: this surfaces through play, not exposition. The world carries its history; the characters move through it. Your job is to place the fragments well, not deliver them efficiently.
What do you do when the world is very certain who you are — and you're not?
Every arc, every faction move, every NPC encounter should, in some way, put pressure on that question. If a session isn't touching it, ask yourself how it could.

Segment 5: The Child & The Old Woman
[These moments emerge naturally from the player's approach in Segment 4. Don't force them; allow them to develop.]
The child watches from behind the woman. Minutes pass. Maybe longer. Time moves differently when you're being evaluated. The child's eyes never quite leave you, tracking movement, cataloging threat.
The child doesn't approach. Stays behind the woman. But the voice carries across the space between you:
"Are you like the ones who burned the village?"
Not accusation. Just need. The real question underneath:
Are you what happened to us?
The Warrior's response to this question sets everything that follows.
How you answer—the words, the tone, whether you make yourself smaller—determines whether the child believes you're safe. And through the child, whether the woman does too.
She doesn't announce herself. One moment you're sitting with the soldier's eyes on you, next there's a bowl. Thin soup. Barely more than water with grain's ghost in it. But hot.
The old woman settles nearby. Not close. Not far. Doesn't ask permission. Doesn't ask questions. Her movements carry the unhurried quality of someone who's made a decision that doesn't require proof.
If you speak, she listens. If you don't, she doesn't press.
Her trust—because that's what it is—arrives like weather. It simply is.
The soldier watches this. Eyes narrow slightly. Not disapproval. Assessment. The old woman's judgment carries weight.
Once the old woman brings food, the woman with the spear sits. Still watching. But the readiness has shifted. Less coiled.
She nods. Small. A signal the camp understands: "The old woman trusts. Maybe we wait."
If the Warrior has built genuine connection by this point—with the child, with the old woman—the soldier becomes something different. Not threat. Ally.
[This should happen once the Warrior has begun establishing some trust. The crisis should feel like a
of that trust, not a betrayal of it.]
Movement at the camp's edge. A scout runs in. Not panicked. Urgent. Blood soaking through her shoulder—not deep but worrying.
"Soldiers," she says. "Imperial patrol. Moving through. Maybe an hour."
The camp moves. Practiced. No panic.
Tents folding. Fires dying. Possessions gathered. Children pulled close. Valuables secured. The choreography of people who've done this before. Who know what happens if they don't.
The woman with the spear looks at you directly.
"We can't fight them. Eight soldiers. We're thirty—most children, most old. Fight, and everyone dies. Run, maybe they let us go. But we need to be ready. Need to be quiet."
"And we need someone watching the perimeter. In case they come from a direction we're not expecting."
Not a question. Assessment. She's asking if you're capable. But also: will you protect through restraint? Or will you be the violence they fear?

Stone beneath your feet. Worn smooth by years of standing watch, or perhaps just worn by your memory of standing watch—hard to tell which came first. The darkness around you isn't empty. It's full of breathing. Thirty people hiding in the ravine behind you, trusting you to be the thing between them and what hunts.

Not soldiers. Not warriors who chose this. Refugees. The old woman who brought you soup without asking questions. The child with eyes too old, who wanted to know if you're like the ones who burned the village. People who didn't ask for this war, this hunt, this fear. They just want to survive another night.
Your duty is simple. Clear. Keep them safe.
The soldiers are close now. You can hear boots testing ground, voices conferring in low tones. Your hand knows the grip. Your body knows the draw. The blade at your hip doesn't sing—it
. One motion and you could end this. One stroke and the threat dissolves.
and your body is screaming that the space between them should be closed. Now. Fast. Final.
Whose voice is this? Whose thirst?

The blade howls but your gut whispers: what about the people behind you? What begins when steel meets steel and thirty terrified souls realize the armed stranger they're hiding with just became the violence they were fleeing?
So you stand. Muscles coiled. Breath controlled. Power surging through you like water behind a dam, and you—you are the dam. You are the choice to hold.
The boots pass. The voices fade. They never knew you were there.
You're still standing. Still holding the flood inside. Still choosing restraint over release.
And somehow—despite every instinct, despite the blade's hunger, despite the screaming need to ACT—
Dawn breaks. The woman with the spear approaches.
The soldiers passed. The camp survived. The Warrior protected through restraint, not force.
She looks at you differently now. Not with fear. Something else entirely.
"Scouts say there's a caravan. Two hours west. Merchants heading for the coastal cities. We're going with them—safer in numbers than out here alone."
"You can fight, can't you? I mean...
This is the moment. She's registering what you are. What you're capable of. But she's not afraid anymore. She's asking if you'll fight
The camp joins the merchant caravan heading west. You're integrated—hired as protection, or invited, or simply absorbed into the group through the old woman's quiet insistence.
You're given a place. A role.
More importantly: you're traveling with people who chose to trust you despite knowing what you carry.
As the caravan settles for evening travel or makes camp:
The other heroes are there. All of them. Same caravan. Together.
Strangers. But something about them feels
in a way you can't name.
When your eyes meet—across the fire, along the caravan route—something resonates.

This awakening is one of six (Breaker, Bridge, Seeker, Sacrificer, Warrior, Visionary). Each happens in parallel, with the GM managing multiple scenes and pacing.
This moment (restraint while watching, as danger passes) is the Warrior's personal revelation. It's theirs alone until they choose to share it. It reinforces their archetype's core doubt:
Can I be strong without being dangerous? Can I protect without controlling?
The Warrior arrives at the caravan as the
only one who has already protected others
. This shapes their relationships with the other heroes. They enter the group with established capability and trust with strangers—a different dynamic than the other archetypes.

Later in Session 0, all six heroes will share a vision at the campfire (Hero Heaven moment). The Warrior's personal relationship with restraint and protection will inform how they interpret that shared vision.

![[narrative/audio/Movement Brings the World In Focus - Warrior.mp3]]
[Context emerges through observation, not explanation. The player discovers the setting by looking.]
As the player rises to sitting (or standing, depending on their choice):

Your movement brings the world into focus piece by piece, each detail arriving like testimony at an inquest. Shapes resolve into shelters—no, not shelters, but a more dolorous architecture. Cloth draped over frames that were never meant to bear weight for this long. The camp nestles into a wound-like depression in the landscape that people have decided to make home. Half-sunk below grade, using the land itself as walls. Whether it's a ravine worn by old water or a drainage cut by someone's labor years ago doesn't matter—what matters is it hides them. From wind, yes. But mostly from predation's gaze. The hunters.

Thirty people, maybe? Hard to count when they're all trying to be so unseen. Fires burning so low they're barely confession, just enough heat to justify the smoke. Tents patched past the point where you could call it repair—this is archaeological layering, strata of fabric and desperation. Some people wrapped in blankets so threadbare they're mere suggestions, light filtering through the weave like broken promises.

Near the closest fire, an old woman worries a pot with movements that refuse to be hurried. Each stir deliberate, patient, as though time itself has agreed to leave her be. She doesn't look up. Doesn't need to—her awareness spreads through posture alone, the way she holds her shoulders, how her stirring never quite falls into rhythm. Listening without seeming to.

Farther out, a woman sits with her back to one of the cloth walls, but she's not resting. Mid-thirties, perhaps. Or maybe younger and aged past her years by whatever put those scars on her forearms. She watches the camp's edges with the kind of systematic scan that comes from training, not fear. Every few seconds her eyes complete a circuit—perimeter, people, perimeter, people: Professional. A soldier's habits wearing civilian clothes.

A child stares in your direction. Five years old, maybe less. Small in the way children are small when they haven't been eating enough, all angles and wide eyes. But those eyes carry something they shouldn't—a wariness that belongs to adults who've learned the world has teeth.
The moment the child registers your consciousness—that shift from still to aware—the child bolts. Not toward safety. Not toward anything. Just
, legs pumping, bare feet finding purchase in the muck that tried to keep you. Running deeper into camp, closer to the woman with the soldier's eyes...
As the child reaches the woman:
Voices spike. Not panic. Commands. Urgency without the pretense of calm. The woman rises in one motion. Hand finds spear. She doesn't point it.
Around the fires, bodies shift. One man stands, gathers his family—wife, two children—moves them back. Not running. Adjusting distance. The way you step away from something unpredictable.
The old woman keeps stirring. Doesn't look. But her shoulders have angled toward you. Listening.
The weight settles. You're the problem. The thing that doesn't belong.
The blade is in your hand. When did you stand? When did your grip tighten? The movement happened without thought. Muscle memory.
It feels right there. Natural. Your body knows this weight.
Instinct screams. Not words. Pressure behind your eyes. The kind that builds when you need to—

Cold comes first—not the clean bite of winter air, but something more claustrophobic and cloying. Something that's settled into your bones like sediment, patient and aching. Your left arm is numb where it's been crushed beneath you dully aching from the weight, and when you try to flex fingers, they move like foreign things, more like distant relatives or belonging to a stranger. How long have you been lying like this?

The smells come next, deep and unbidden but a necessary evil of your haggard breathing. They are layered like a burial: unwashed bodies pressed too close. Smoke—cooking fires, low and abashed, nothing eager about them. Lower still, grain gone sour, rotting from the inside out. And underneath
, sharp and copper-bright: fear-sweat. That particular reek of people who understand, deeply, the necessity of caution, and the peerless value of being small. What it means to be hunted.

The wind, because of course, there is a breeze you realize, carries with it sounds in fragments. You can feel it as much as hear it, touching your skin and tickling your ears. A child crying somewhere distant—not the thin wail of hunger, but something quieter. Self-aware enough at whatever young age to somehow know it shouldn't cry too loud. Fire crackling, but subdued, speaking in whispers. Voices urgent and careful. Footsteps on packed earth, deliberately slow. The shuffle of people who have learned to move as though apology itself has weight.

Darkness greets you—not absence of light but a thickness to the air itself, like looking through cloth. Shapes emerge slowly: angles that might be shelters, humps that could be sleeping bodies or discarded bundles. And beneath you, pressing against your cheek, the mud.

This isn't the honest mud of a riverbank that dries clean in sun. This is earth that's given up. Degraded past soil into something closer to rot—compacted by years of feet that had nowhere else to stand, stained by blood washed thin until it forgot it was ever red, host to whatever got dropped and never retrieved
because retrieval meant admitting you'd lost something worth keeping
. Your left arm sinks into it past the wrist, skin bonded to cold wetness like an unwelcome embrace from a cold lover, a pact you don't remember making. Something solid rests against the pulse point.

You move to lift your arm, half in recoil and half for balance and the movement costs you. As the muscles pull and the slow sucking sound of muck challenging your release from its intimate embrace you feel the solid thing's weight shift and for a moment—just a moment—you feel it resist. A shy partner, unconvinced of the wooing. But move it does.

A blade emerges with your arm, trailing streamers of muck. Simple and dark—the kind of crude iron that was never meant to catch light and throw it back. No shine of care, no gleam of pride. Just function hammered into shape by someone who knew what they were doing but didn't waste time making it pretty. The grip is bone wrapped in leather gone the color of old bruises, the kind that yellow at the edges when they're trying to heal. A leather thong cinches it to your wrist, tight enough to announce itself with every pulse but not quite tight enough to numb. The blade itself carries stains that might be rust. Or might be something that
rust before it decided to become a question.

You look at it—this... this tool. This rudimentary expression of violence and mis-repair, that you apparently brought to whatever this place is—and the first thought that surfaces isn't relief. Not recognition either, though something about the weight feels
in a way that bypasses memory entirely. Just a certainty that arrives simple and terrible and absolute:
The woman approaches. Not fast. Not slow. Measured. Each step deliberate, weight tested before commitment. Hand still on the spear. Eyes locked.
Two words. Not a threat. Not a request. Just information. Here's what happens next if you do.
From deeper in camp, voices. Fragments. They're not trying to whisper—they're trying to decide.
One voice, older, cuts through: "Keep the children back."
Twenty feet away, the woman drops into a crouch. Combat stance. Ready to spring, ready to dodge. Weight on the balls of her feet.
She waits. Doesn't advance. Doesn't retreat. Watching.
"I'm going to ask you something," she says. Her voice is level. Controlled. "Think hard before you answer."
The whole camp watches. Even the old woman has stopped stirring.
